text: For a moment he wondered whether his son would soften. <break time="0.8s" /> And come back with the dogs. <break time="0.8s" /> To take him along. <break time="0.8s" /> But he soon let the thought go. <break time="0.8s" /> Because he knew. <break time="0.8s" /> That this was the law. <break time="0.8s" /> Of all living things. <break time="0.8s" /> Nature did not care about a single life. <break time="0.8s" /> And the only task. <break time="0.8s" /> That she gave to every creature. <break time="0.8s" /> Was to have young ones. <break time="0.8s" /> When that task was done. <break time="0.8s" /> Death came. <break time="0.8s" /> And this was the rule. <break time="0.8s" /> That every creature had to obey. <break time="0.8s" /> In the end. <break time="0.8s" /> The mosquito vanished. <break time="0.8s" /> With the first frost. <break time="0.8s" /> And the little tree squirrel crept away. <break time="0.8s" /> To die alone. <break time="0.8s" /> The old rabbit grew too slow. <break time="0.8s" /> To run from its enemies. <break time="0.8s" /> And even the great bear. <break time="0.8s" /> Became blind and clumsy at last. <break time="0.8s" /> In his strong years. <break time="0.8s" /> He had led his people as their chief. <break time="0.8s" /> And he too had once made a hard choice. <break time="0.8s" /> Like his sons. <break time="0.8s" /> Long ago one winter before the missionary came. <break time="0.8s" /> He had left his own father behind. <break time="0.8s" /> On an upper reach of the Klondike. <break time="0.8s" /> It was not cruelty. <break time="0.8s" /> That made him do it. <break time="0.8s" /> But the same law. <break time="0.8s" /> That now left him alone by the fire.
